newsitem.title: USA: Japan, debt news boost Russia at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Japan, debt news boost Russia at G7 summit.

text.p: Russia, marking the Group of Seven summit with a flurry of diplomatic moves, promised on Friday to stop pointing missiles at China and Japan and won a chance of getting back money lent to allies in the Soviet era.

Kremlin officials said Russian President Boris Yeltsin would set up a telephone hotline with Pacific neighbour Japan and a Japanese spokesman said there would be regular bilateral summits with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said Russia -- a big debtor in its own right -- had been admitted to the Paris Club of creditor nations as a creditor state.
"I'm very pleased," Clinton told reporters at the start of a meeting with Yeltsin.
"What you see here is a sweeping integration of Russia into the major decision-making networks of the world in a way that is very positive for the rest of us."

Russia's full integration into the industrialised world's political and economic institutions had been Yeltsin's main aim at the summit, attended by the leaders of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
Yeltsin will attend most of the talks, but will be excluded from an hour's session on financial and macro-economic issues.

Decades of frosty ties with Japan had long been a stumbling block and Tokyo officials have been reluctant to contemplate Russia joining the G7 until a long-running dispute over the status of a group of Pacific islands was solved.
Japan says the islands, seized by the Soviet army in the closing days of the Second World War, must be handed back.
Yeltsin, aware that territorial concessions would prompt a fierce backlash from his nationalist opponents, says there is no question of returning what Russia calls the Kurile Islands.
The dispute has prevented the two states from signing a formal peace treaty ending wartime hostilities.

A Japanese foreign ministry official said the territorial dispute would not be settled in the near future, but the new initiatives on a hotline and summit meetings clearly put ties between the two countries on a much better footing.
"It is quite a big step," the official told a news briefing. "Two flows are merging into one flow."
The official also said that Yeltsin, in a goodwill gesture, had promised to stop pointing missiles against China and Japan, although he said he was not sure what this meant.

"As an act of goodwill, the missiles have been de-targeted from such counries as the United States, Britain, Germany, France. Now is the time to completely detarget them from countries like Japan and China," he said, quoting Yeltsin.
The announcement about missiles appeared to be mainly of symbolic value, rather than pointing to a new policy thrust.

Yeltsin said last month that Russia would stop targeting missiles at NATO states. Experts said it would be relatively quick and easy to reprogram the computers on the missiles to change this policy again.
Japan is not a NATO member, but U.S. troops are based on Japanese territory.

Russia, which inherited the debts and the liabilities of the former Soviet Union, has also been seeking a bigger global economic role. But officials said last week that Paris Club membership would not come at the G7 summit and they were expected to be pleased at the announcement.

Russia has already won deals to reschedule its own multi-billion dollar debts. But Moscow also lent large sums to Soviet-era allies in the developing world and officials see Paris Club membership as a way to get some of that back.
